title: On the phone
job: Calls and messages — openings, closings, taking a message
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

allowedPatterns: Il n'est pas là + . + Je peux laisser un message?

rules.text: FRENCH HAS NO CONTINUOUS TENSE. Je parle covers "I speak" and "I am speaking" alike, so a learner reaching for an -ing equivalent finds none. être en train de parler exists and is emphatic — right in the middle of it — rather than the default. Italian's answer to the same problem is the opposite one, and a call is where both languages show their hand.

Allô? answers a phone and nothing else. It is not a greeting at a door and not a way of getting someone's attention. The identification is C'est Marc à l'appareil, where L1-M8's c'est does the work and à l'appareil is what makes it a phone call.

This module speaks vous throughout, for a reason worth stating plainly: you cannot see who picked up. M6's tu is deliberately absent, and that is a rule about not knowing rather than about politeness.

SPOKEN FRENCH DROPS THE ne — Il est pas là, Je sais pas — and this course writes it everywhere, in display, forms and pool alike. Writing both would fork one negation into two index surfaces. A phone call is where a learner first hears the drop, so it is named here and in no other module.

Taking a message needs no new tense: laisser un message, rappeler, le numéro, Ne quittez pas, and L1-M5's passé composé for what already happened — Il a appelé. Reported speech, Il a dit que…, is L3's, which is why a message is passed on with the words themselves.

words.note: Only on a phone. Bonjour is for meeting someone, and using either in the other place is heard at once.
Literally "at the device". The elision fuses l' onto the noun, so the whole thing is one index key with the bare word beside it.

sentences.trap: Je suis Marc is what a learner reaches for and it sounds like an introduction at a door. On a phone French says C'est, exactly as English says "this is".
sentences.sound: a-LO say MARK a la-pa-RAY. The circumflex on ô says the vowel is closed and long.

variations.changed: just the answer, which is what a person picking up says

mistake.display: Allô? Je suis Marc à l'appareil
mistake.why: On a phone French uses c'est: C'est Marc à l'appareil.

sentences.usage: Both ends of every call in French start here.
sentences.mnemonic: Allô is only ever a phone.

sentences.cue: I'd like to speak to Anne

words.note: The infinitive behind L1-M5's parlé. It takes à with a person and nothing with a language — parler à Anne, parler français.
A phone number, a house number, a size. The é is a letter with its accent, and the o at the end is closed.

sentences.trap: parler takes à with a person and no preposition at all with a language. parler avec exists and means talking WITH someone rather than to them, which is a different conversation.
sentences.sound: zhuh voo-DRAY par-LAY a AN. The infinitive and the participle parlé sound identical.

variations.cue: I'd like to speak to Marc

mistake.why: A person takes à: Je voudrais parler à Anne.

sentences.usage: Asking for someone when a third person answers.
sentences.mnemonic: parler à a person, parler a language.

words.note: ne plus est, fused by the elision into one token. L1-M5 showed the same join in n'ai, and the index sees a single key.
The accent is the whole difference from L1-M1's la, the article. It covers "there" and often "here" — Il est là means he is in.

sentences.trap: là and la are one accent apart and the accent is a letter. The index treats them as two keys, and only one of them means anything about place.
sentences.sound: eel neh pa LA. The n' is elided onto the verb and the whole line runs flat.

variations.display: Il n'est pas là. Je peux laisser un message?
variations.cue: He isn't here. Can I leave a message?

mistake.why: The place word carries an accent: Il n'est pas là.

sentences.usage: Answering a call for someone who is out.
sentences.mnemonic: The accent is what makes it a place.

words.note: Leaving a thing behind, not leaving a place — that is partir, L1-M6's verb. The double s is a hiss.
Masculine, and both g sounds are soft. Un message is what you leave; le numéro is what you leave with it.

sentences.trap: This is a question made by intonation alone. The words are a statement, and French asks a great many questions this way — M1's est-ce que is the other option and is not compulsory.
sentences.sound: zhuh puh leh-SAY un meh-SAZH. The final g of message is the soft zh.

variations.display: Est-ce que je peux laisser un message?

variations.changed: the offer rather than the request

mistake.why: An infinitive follows peux: Je peux laisser un message?

sentences.usage: When the person you wanted is out.

sentences.display: Ne quittez pas, s'il vous plaît

words.note: Literally "do not leave". It is the fixed phrase for holding a line and is almost never heard outside it.

sentences.trap: The negation wraps the verb: ne in front, pas behind. It is L1-M3's own frame, and the imperative changes nothing about where the two halves go.
sentences.sound: nuh kee-TAY pa. The whole phrase runs as one and the final s of pas is silent.

variations.display: Ne quittez pas, je vous rappelle
variations.cue: Hold the line — I'll call you back

mistake.display: Ne pas quittez, s'il vous plaît
mistake.why: The negation wraps the verb: Ne quittez pas, s'il vous plaît.

sentences.usage: Holding someone while you fetch another person.
sentences.mnemonic: ne in front, pas behind, always.

sentences.cue: I'll call you back this evening

words.note: appeler with ra- on the front, which means again. The double l appears only where the ending is silent — je rappelle but rappeler.

sentences.trap: This is a present tense doing the work of English's future, and the time word carries the rest. Je vous rappellerai exists and would sound like a promise about next month.
sentences.sound: zhuh voo ra-PEL suh SWAR. The double l is where the stress of the word sits.

variations.cue: I'll call you back this evening

variations.changed: asking rather than promising, with the infinitive

mistake.why: The pronoun goes in front: Je vous rappelle ce soir.

sentences.usage: Closing a call you could not finish.

words.note: The participle of appeler, and it is what passes a message on. With avoir it does not agree with anything, which M10 will state as a rule.
L1-M4 taught le matin, mornings in general; this is the one that has just happened. Both are whole surfaces and neither answers for the other.

sentences.trap: L1-M5's past does the whole job here. French has no separate way of reporting what someone said at this level, and Il a dit que… belongs to L3 — so a message travels in the words it arrived in.
sentences.sound: eel a a-puh-LAY suh ma-TAN. Two a's meet in the middle and both are sounded.

mistake.why: With avoir the participle does not agree: Il a appelé ce matin.

sentences.usage: Telling someone who rang while they were out.

words.note: One form for both. French has no continuous tense at all, so nothing in the sentence says whether this is a habit or is happening now.

sentences.trap: There is no way to mark "right now" here, and none is needed. A learner hunting for an -ing form will not find one, and adding en train de would make the sentence emphatic rather than ordinary.
sentences.sound: zhuh PARL a-VEK AN. parle ends in a consonant cluster with no vowel after it.

mistake.why: French has no continuous: Je parle avec Anne.

sentences.usage: Saying what is going on — and the same words would do for a habit.
sentences.mnemonic: One present for both English presents.

words.note: The infinitive, with a single l because the ending is sounded. Vous pouvez me rappeler? is the request that uses it.

sentences.trap: bon goes in FRONT of the noun, because it is on M3's short list. Most adjectives would follow, and this one does not.
sentences.sound: say luh bon nü-may-RO. The ü of numéro is rounded.

variations.display: Ce n'est pas le bon numéro

mistake.why: bon is on the front list: C'est le bon numéro?

sentences.usage: Checking a number you were given, or one that came up wrong.
sentences.mnemonic: bon goes in front, like beau.

words.note: Un moment holds someone for a few seconds. Un instant does the same and is slightly more formal.

sentences.trap: Salut is for people you address as tu, and on a phone you do not know who answered. Au revoir is the safe close, exactly as vous is the safe address.
sentences.sound: mer-SEE o ruh-VWAR. The r's are at the back of the throat.

mistake.why: On a vous call the close is au revoir: Merci, au revoir.

sentences.usage: Ending a call with anyone you would address as vous.
sentences.mnemonic: au revoir on a phone, always.
